analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and funds them with taxes on high earners and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote or a hearing: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security benefits for current and future beneficiaries, set a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for people who worked many years at low wages, base cost-of-living increases on an index that tracks what seniors actually buy, and let children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers keep collecting benefits through age 22 while in school. It pays for this by applying Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above the current cap up to $250,000, raising the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%, and applying that tax to active business income. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries across the board, especially low-lifetime earners who would get a minimum benefit at or above the poverty line, seniors whose cost-of-living adjustments would rise faster, and full-time students up to 22 whose parents received retirement or disability benefits or who lost a parent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, disabled workers, low earners, students

how_it_helps.text: It raises the benefit formula by moving the replacement rate on the first tier of earnings from 90% to 95% and adding a 22% increase to the first bend point, which raises monthly checks for beneficiaries.

It creates a new minimum benefit for long-term low earners: a person with 11 years of work would get at least a small percentage of the poverty guideline, scaled up to 125% of the poverty guideline for someone with 30 or more years of work.

It switches cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, an index that reflects the spending patterns of older households, which tend to include a larger share of health care costs.

It lets children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers who are full-time students receive benefits until age 22 instead of ending at 19, and makes the same change under the Railroad Retirement Act.

It pays for the expansion by applying the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above the current cap (about $160,000 in 2023) up to $250,000, and by raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% while making active business income subject to it; 62% of that investment tax goes to the Social Security trust fund.
It merges the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners who make more than the current payroll tax cap, and high-income households with investment income or business income, who would pay the new and higher taxes that fund the benefit increases.

drawbacks.text: The bill would substantially raise taxes on high earners and on investment and business income, lifting the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% and extending it to active trade or business income.

Applying the payroll tax to earnings between the current cap and $250,000 raises taxes on workers and self-employed people in that income band, with the employer share likely passed along in compensation over time.
The benefit increases are permanent spending that the new taxes would need to cover indefinitely; if the taxes raised less than projected, the trust fund would still face pressure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and concrete: bigger checks, a poverty-level floor for long-career low earners, faster cost-of-living adjustments, and longer support for students. The cost is concentrated on households with high wages or significant investment and business income. Whether that trade is worth it is a values question; the design question is whether the new taxes would reliably cover the permanent benefit growth, which the bill's own funding structure assumes they would.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 13, 2023, with ten Democratic senators as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and households with large investment or business income, who would have paid the new taxes, are better off because the bill died in committee; so is anyone who preferred the current financing and benefit structure unchanged.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chairs, received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the Independent sponsor; no Republicans supported it, and no roll call ever occurred because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would nearly quintuple the net investment income tax (from 3.8% to 16.2%) and apply the Social Security payroll tax to wages above the current cap up to $250,000, with the proceeds funding higher benefits for ordinary beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Owners of active businesses and pass-through income
industries.note: Active trade or business income, currently exempt from the net investment income tax, would become subject to the 16.2% tax.
